messages:
Aisha: Thanks for the all-hands — quick follow-up on some runtime tradeoffs. We have a couple teams trying to hit a 90th pct SLO ~150ms while also supporting higher QPS. Do you have concrete guidance for when to pick strict latency routing vs enabling larger batching/prefix caching? Also curious on kernel prioritization: are we focusing long-seq attention kernels first or KV/cache improvements? cc @Gabe @Lina

Gabe: Short answer: it depends on the customer tier and p99 tolerance. If you must hit 150ms 90th, favor low-latency routing + smaller batches + cached prefixes. For throughput-focused workloads where 95/99 can be higher, enable batch-optimized routes. We plan to publish a simple decision tree in the docs by EOW. :spiral_calendar:

Lina: One nuance on kernels: long-seq attention optimizations help when median/mean token length > ~512 (e.g., code completions, long docs). KV cache improvements give wins for short-turn dialog workloads with repeated prefixes. We're parallelizing both but the next release prioritizes long-seq kernels on A100/8 because the perf delta is largest there. KV work is gated on the cache API stability RFC.

Aisha: Helpful — can teams rely on automatic routing? Is there a default policy we should use for mid-market customers?

Gabe: Yes, we have a default routing profile: low-latency primary, batch-optimized fallback, with automatic prefix-caching enabled for routes that show >30% prefix reuse. For mid-market we recommend starting with the default then tuning batch_size and max_latency_ms once you have 24–72h of telemetry.

Lina: Example config we use internally (pseudocode):
```
route:
  primary: low-latency
  fallback: batch-optimized
  batching:
    max_batch_size: 16
    max_latency_ms: 8
    allow_prefix_cache: true
```
If you need lower latency reduce max_batch_size and max_latency_ms; for higher throughput bump them up.

Marco: From PM side: if you're deciding for a GA feature, prioritize predictable latency for UX-critical flows (search, checkout, auth prompts). For background/async workloads (vectorizing docs, offline summarization) favor throughput. We'll add a short checklist to the all-hands follow-up doc.

Ravi: Ops note: enabling larger batches can increase token concurrency which affects GPU memory pressure. If you switch a route to batch-optimized, make sure to check per-GPU mem utilization on the console and set a conservative autoscale min_replicas for the first 24h. Also watch queue depth metrics; when queue grows >0.5s average we recommend lowering batch window.

Aisha: Makes sense. On kernel timelines — any ETA for the long-seq kernel release we can cite in customer comms?

Lina: Public ETA: internal canary mid-next-week, gradual rollout over 3 weeks assuming no regressions. If you need tighter dates for customer comms ping me and I'll share the canary plan.

Gabe: Also want to call out Redwood Optimize's new suggestion engine — it can auto-propose batch/config changes based on a 48h telemetry window. Use that as a starting point, not a hard rule.

Jess: I'll add a short KB in Console > Runtime > Recommendations with example configs and a one-pager for sales to reference.

Aisha: Thanks all. Can we set up a 30-minute sync for technical leads tomorrow to go over a couple of customer cases?

eng-bot: Meeting scheduled: runtime-slo-batching-sync — tomorrow 10:00am PT. Invite sent to participants. :calendar:

Gabe: Thanks — Lina/Ravi/Jess, please join and bring any canary dashboards you have.

Lina: Will do. I'll bring canary perf traces and a short perf vs mem table.

Ravi: I'll bring scaling notes and a short checklist for safe rollout.

Aisha: Great, appreciate it. :thumbsup:
